name: Vera Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, walk me through a normal working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior cook at Fuoco, a pizza and pasta place that's packed in the evenings and does even more through the delivery apps. I'm on pasta, boiling, tossing, finishing sauces, and when it's quiet I help stretch dough. There's a tablet by the pass with all the app orders pinging, and somehow I became the one who sorts it out. My pasta's still a bit uneven, Chef Bruno tells me that every night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like puzzles, and a Friday night with forty app orders is a puzzle. I use AI every day, I even got it to predict how much dough we need from last year's numbers, and it's better than Bruno's guess. What wears me out is the Sunday double and standing on tile for ten hours. I live on my own in a small flat, my sister's round the corner, and I've got about four months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool and people got carried away. I'd still post about the dough forecast, because it saved us binning trays of dough. Useful, not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it changes nothing for me, which is fine. Fuoco's busy, my pay's normal, my rent's okay. I'd just keep learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep at the pasta until Bruno stops complaining. Offer to handle more of the stock ordering with the tools, since I'm already good at it. Keep saving, maybe take a short course in kitchen management online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly restless, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Restless how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want something to aim at. If AI doesn't change kitchens, I'd want to move up the normal way, sous chef, then maybe my own place. That's ten years of Sunday doubles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything about money that worries you, even now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Four months is decent for me, and my sister's close if something goes wrong. The flat's small but cheap.

say: AI is a **decent tool**, and people got **carried away**.
The **dough forecast** saved us binning trays, so it's useful, not magic.
think: It changes **nothing for me**, and that's fine.
Fuoco is busy, my pay is normal and my **rent** is manageable, so I'd **keep learning**.
do: Even out my **pasta** until the head chef stops complaining.
Take on more **stock ordering** using AI tools.
Do a short online **kitchen management** course.
S0.quote: If AI doesn't change kitchens, I'd want to move up the normal way, sous chef, then maybe my own place.
fieldNote: Vera is a **daily AI user** who already handles the kitchen's app **orders**.
Her money feels **secure**: low rent, four months saved, a sister nearby.
Without change she'd climb the **slow traditional ladder**, which makes her restless.

steps.text: Keep working the pasta station and even out portions
Take over Fuoco's stock ordering using AI forecasts
Do a short online course in kitchen management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small places that adapt will be fine and the ones that don't will struggle. I'd say it to Bruno, actually, gently. I'd tell friends to get good with the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the app orders and stock ordering are exactly the thinking bits that go to software, and I'm the one doing them. That's either my promotion or my job disappearing, depending on how I play it. The cooking stays human for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up the AI ordering properly at Fuoco and make myself the person who runs it, even if I have to do a short course on the software. I'd ask Bruno for a small raise for it within the year. If he says no, I'd take it to a bigger group that's hiring for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. I like that I can see it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Bruno says the software means he doesn't need anyone on the tablet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I go back to just pasta, which I'm not great at yet, and that's the risk. So I'd want to be useful twice, cooking and running the system. I'd practise pasta harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Fuoco would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia on front of house, she answers the phone and takes bookings. That goes straight to software in this picture. I'd tell her to learn the booking system before they replace her with it.

I'd tell friends to get **good with the tools**.

It's my **promotion** or my job vanishing, depending on how I play it.

Ask the head chef for a **small raise** for it within a year.
Move to a **bigger group** if he says no.
feel: **Uneasy but excited**, because I can see it coming.

fieldNote: She spots that her **thinking tasks** are the exposed part, not her cooking.

steps.text: Set up and run the AI ordering system at Fuoco

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, we can't stop it, so let's be smart about it. I'd say governments and businesses both need to move fast. Not much use shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, by 2028 the AI does everything I do on the tablet, better. Then 2031, robots that can toss pasta. I'd be thirty-two, with good tech skills and average cooking skills. I think I'd land somewhere, but probably not in a kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now learning how kitchen robots are installed and run, there are online courses already. By 2029 I'd try to get a job with a company that sets up robot kitchens for restaurants. I'd save more, aim for six months, because there might be a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more curious than scared. I'm single, I've got no kids, I can move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move cities for that kind of job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in a heartbeat. My sister would miss me. But that's the advantage of being twenty-seven with a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Bruno?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That he should get the robots before the chain down the road does, honestly. Fuoco can't afford to be last. Bruno would hate hearing it.

say: It's here and we can't stop it, so let's be **smart** about it.
**Governments and businesses** both need to move fast.
think: By 2028 the AI does all my **tablet work** better than me.
With **robots by 2031**, I'd likely land work outside kitchens.
do: Take online courses in **installing kitchen robots** now.
Join a **robot kitchen** set-up company by 2029.
Save toward **six months** in case of a gap.
S2.quote: I'm single, I've got no kids, I can move.
fieldNote: She sees her **tablet work** going first and her cooking three years later.
Being single and young makes **moving for work** easy for her.
She'd advise her own boss to **automate early**, knowing he'd hate it.

steps.text: Take online courses on running kitchen robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you're paying attention. I'd tell people at work to use the time, learn the systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AGI in 2031 and robots in 2034 is a good timeline for me. I'd have time to be sous chef, then become the person who runs the robot side of a kitchen group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run Fuoco's ordering on AI from next year. Get to sous chef in three years. Around 2032 learn the robot systems properly, and pitch myself to a group as their kitchen tech lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit uneasy, because it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a kitchen tech lead do, in your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Makes sure the machines, the ordering and the cooks all work together. Fixes small things, calls in big repairs. Someone who knows both food and tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Are you sure that job will exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not sure. But every new machine needs someone to look after it at first. If it doesn't exist, I'll make the case for it.

I'd tell workmates to use the time to **learn the systems**.
think: AGI in 2031 and **robots in 2034** is a good timeline for me.
I'd have time to make **sous chef**, then run a kitchen group's **robot side**.
do: Run Fuoco's **ordering on AI** from next year.
Pitch myself as a group's **kitchen tech lead** around 2032.

S3.quote: Every new machine needs someone to look after it at first.
fieldNote: Five years turns the change into a **career opportunity** for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so stop worrying and start learning. I'd probably post a little thread about how kitchens could look in 2040.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd love it. Ten years to grow, then robots in 2039 when I'm forty and maybe running my own place. I'd buy the robots myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the cooking properly for five years, then save to open a small pasta bar around 2035. Keep using AI for everything I can. When robots come, I'd automate the boring parts and keep the fun bits human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your own pasta bar. How would you pay for it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Savings, a small loan, maybe my sister as a partner, she's in accounts. I'd start tiny, ten seats and delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hire cooks, if robots can do the line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few, for the parts guests care about, like finishing the dish at the counter. I'd rather pay two good cooks well than ten badly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have to jump before I've learned to cook properly. What would help is cheap short courses on running kitchen robots, and restaurants being willing to train their own staff instead of hiring outsiders.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what cooks would actually like robots to do. Nobody wants to peel forty kilos of onions. If the robots take the onions and leave us the cooking, fine.

Her **centre** outlook is pragmatic: adapt fast rather than shout.
She ranges from **calm** in AI Plateau and AGI by 2036 to **anxious** in AGI by 2028.
